q: A grower standing on Atlas Peak looks west across the valley floor to Mount Veeder on the opposite skyline. Napa is walled in by which two ranges?
opts: The Santa Lucia and the Gabilan
The Sierra Nevada and the Mayacamas
The Cascades and the Coast Range
exp: The Mayacamas divide Napa from Sonoma on the west and carry Mount Veeder and Spring Mountain, while the Vaca range on the east carries Atlas Peak and Howell Mountain. The valley narrows steadily as it runs north toward Calistoga.

q: Fog funnels in off the Pacific each night and burns off late the following morning, which has made one Sonoma appellation a byword for Pinot Noir. Which?
exp: The fog buys several extra hours of cool each day, stretching the ripening period. That long, slow hang is what growers there are really farming for.

q: Old head-trained bush vines of Zinfandel are the signature of which Sonoma appellation?
opts: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
exp: Dry Creek's warm days and gravelly benchland suit Zinfandel, and some plantings there date back over a century. Old vines yield little but concentrate flavour.

q: Which Sonoma appellation, warmer and further from the ocean, has built its name on rounded Cabernet Sauvignon?
opts: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
exp: Alexander Valley runs north from Healdsburg and sits beyond the reach of most of the fog. Its Cabernet tends to be softer and earlier drinking than Napa's.

q: A cool valley in Mendocino County, open to the Pacific at its western end, has become a source of traditional method sparkling wine. Name it.
exp: Anderson Valley is cold enough to ripen base wine at low sugar and high acid, which is exactly what sparkling production wants. It is also strong territory for Pinot Noir and aromatic whites.

q: Which North Coast county lies inland and north of Napa, high around a large lake, and contains the Red Hills AVA?
exp: Lake County sits at elevation around Clear Lake, with volcanic soils and very clear air. Its Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc are increasingly bottled under their own labels rather than sold off.

q: Sonoma, Napa, Mendocino and Lake counties all sit inside which umbrella appellation?
exp: North Coast is a large multi-county AVA that also takes in Marin and Solano. Producers reach for it when a blend crosses county lines.

q: In one California county the coastal mountains run east to west rather than north to south, opening the valleys straight at the ocean. What does that do?
opts: Cold marine air pours far inland, so the coastal end is the cold end
It shelters the vineyards from wind entirely
It blocks ocean influence and leaves the valleys uniformly hot
exp: The transverse ranges of Santa Barbara County create a sharp temperature gradient over a short distance. Pinot Noir grows at the western end while Bordeaux varieties ripen at the eastern end.

q: Which Santa Barbara appellation occupies the cold western end of the Santa Ynez Valley and is planted overwhelmingly to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay?
exp: Sta. Rita Hills takes the full force of the marine air coming through the gap. Happy Canyon, further east and much warmer, grows Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc instead.

q: A warm inland appellation in San Luis Obispo County, known for a very wide swing between day and night temperatures, has made its name with Zinfandel and Rhone varieties. Which?
exp: Paso Robles is hot by day and cools sharply after dark, which keeps acidity in place while sugars build. It is large and varied enough to have been divided into a set of sub-appellations.

q: Which county's Salinas Valley draws such a reliable afternoon wind off the bay that growers plan the vineyard around it?
exp: The valley opens directly onto Monterey Bay, and the wind can shut the vines down in the afternoon. The Santa Lucia Highlands sit on terraces above the valley floor and are a leading source of Pinot Noir.

q: Warm, flat and dependent on irrigation, the Central Valley supplies most of the country's everyday wine. Which of these appellations lies within it?
exp: Lodi sits at the northern end, cooled a little by air off the Sacramento Delta. Alongside its volume production it holds a remarkable stock of old Zinfandel vines.

q: Gold Rush miners planted vines in the hills east of Sacramento, and some of those old Zinfandel plantings still stand. Which region is this?
exp: Amador County and El Dorado are the best known parts, farming at elevation on granitic soils. The vineyards survived largely because the area was too remote to be worth redeveloping.

q: DNA analysis matched California's Zinfandel to an old Croatian variety and to which Italian grape?
exp: Zinfandel, Primitivo and the Croatian Tribidrag are one variety under three names. The Croatian population is the original, and the vine reached America by way of a nineteenth-century nursery.

q: A pale, off-dry pink wine made from a black grape became a runaway commercial success in the 1980s. What was it called?
exp: Sutter Home's version began with a fermentation that stopped early and left sugar behind. Its enormous sales are the reason a great many old Zinfandel vineyards were never pulled out.

q: Spanish missionaries brought north the first wine grape to be planted widely in California. What is it known as?
exp: The Mission grape is the Spanish Listan Prieto, carried up from Mexico with the mission chain. It makes rather thin wine and survives now mostly as a curiosity and in some old field blends.
